blueprint_concepts: Pair of straight lines: homogeneous second-degree equation and component slopes
General second-degree equation representing a pair of lines (abc + 2fgh - af^2 - bg^2 - ch^2 = 0)

concept_use.Pair of straight lines: homogeneous seco: The homogeneous part 2x^2 + 5xy + 2y^2 = (2x+y)(x+2y) gives the component slopes and the form of the two lines.
concept_use.General second-degree equation represent: The condition abc + 2fgh - af^2 - bg^2 - ch^2 = 0 (equivalently matching coefficients) gives the two admissible values of alpha.

english: Let $\alpha$ be a real number such that the equation $2x^2+5xy+2y^2+5x+\alpha y+2=0$ represents a pair of straight lines that intersect at a point of the $y$-axis. Then the area of the triangle formed by these two lines and the $x$-axis is
hindi: माना $\alpha$ एक वास्तविक संख्या है जिसके लिए समीकरण $2x^2+5xy+2y^2+5x+\alpha y+2=0$ सरल रेखाओं के एक युग्म को निरूपित करता है जो $y$-अक्ष के एक बिन्दु पर प्रतिच्छेद करती हैं। तब इन दोनों रेखाओं तथा $x$-अक्ष से बने त्रिभुज का क्षेत्रफल है
solution: Homogeneous part $2x^2+5xy+2y^2=(2x+y)(x+2y)$ (slopes $-2,-\frac12$), so the lines are $(2x+y+p)(x+2y+q)=0$
$(p,q)=(1,2)$, $\alpha=4$: lines meet at $(0,-1)$ on the $y$-axis; $(p,q)=(4,\frac12)$, $\alpha=\frac{17}2$: they meet at $\left(-\frac52,1\right)$, rejected
solution_full: The second-degree terms factor as $2x^2+5xy+2y^2=(2x+y)(x+2y)$, so the two lines have slopes $-2$ and $-\frac12$ and can be written as $(2x+y+p)(x+2y+q)=0$.
Expanding: $2x^2+5xy+2y^2+(2q+p)x+(q+2p)y+pq=0$. Comparing with the given equation: $2q+p=5$, $pq=2$, $q+2p=\alpha$.

The same values follow from the condition $abc+2fgh-af^2-bg^2-ch^2=0$ with $a=2,h=\frac52,b=2,g=\frac52,f=\frac{\alpha}{2},c=2$: it reduces to $2\alpha^2-25\alpha+68=0$, so $\alpha=4$ or $\alpha=\frac{17}{2}$.
Case $q=2,p=1,\alpha=4$: lines $2x+y+1=0$ and $x+2y+2=0$. Their intersection: $y=-1-2x$, $x-2-4x+2=0\Rightarrow x=0$, so $(0,-1)$, on the $y$-axis.
Case $q=\frac12,p=4,\alpha=\frac{17}{2}$: lines $2x+y+4=0$ and $x+2y+\frac12=0$ meet at $\left(-\frac52,1\right)$, not on the $y$-axis. Rejected.
So $\alpha=4$. The lines cut the $x$-axis at $\left(-\frac12,0\right)$ and $(-2,0)$, and meet at $(0,-1)$.
originality_note: New: the unknown coefficient has two admissible values from the pair-of-lines condition, and the position of the point of intersection selects one before a triangle is formed (way 3). Closest known: 'find lambda so that the equation represents a pair of lines'. Different because: Delta = 0 gives two values and the factorisation through the component slopes is needed to locate the vertex and choose.

Checked that exactly one of the two admissible alpha gives an intersection on the y-axis. Changed: No change.
key_step: Factorising through the homogeneous part (slopes -2 and -1/2) and choosing the alpha whose lines meet on the y-axis.
justification: Routine pair-of-lines technique with a selection and a simple area; several standard steps, no insight. Comparable to the routine chains rated 2 (2025-P2-Q4, L2).
